name: Peru
summary: A republic on the Pacific coast of South America, independent from Spain since 1821, home to the former heartland of the Inca Empire.

knownFor.label: Ceviche
knownFor.note: Raw fish cured in lime juice, a national dish.

knownFor.label: Machu Picchu
knownFor.note: Inca site made world-famous after 1911; now Peru’s most visited place.

knownFor.label: Guano boom
knownFor.note: Bird droppings sold as fertiliser made Peru rich in the mid-1800s.

location.value: Western South America on the Pacific; about 1.29 million km², the third largest country in South America.

terrain.value: A dry coastal desert, the high Andes and the Amazon rainforest.

climate.value: A dry coast with moderate temperatures; colder highlands up to the frozen Andes peaks; a hot, very rainy Amazon.

resources.value: Copper, gold, zinc, silver and other metals; rich fishing waters; guano was a key export in the 19th century.

urbanisation.value: Lima is the capital and largest city.

disease.value: Peru had the highest COVID-19 death rate in the world.

migration.value: Chinese and Japanese labourers arrived from the 1850s; European immigrants after independence; more than 10% of Peruvians now live abroad.

economicBase.value: Mining, manufacturing, agriculture, fishing and tourism.

tradeRoutes.value: Main trade partners are the United States, China, Brazil and Chile.

moneyAndTax.value: The sol, replaced by the inti (1985) and the nuevo sol (1991) after chronic inflation; inflation reached 7,650% in 1990.

inequality.value: High inequality persisted even after the economic reforms of the 1990s.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic; the army ruled after the 1968 coup.

keyRulers.value: Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín (independence). Ramón Castilla. Juan Velasco Alvarado. Alberto Fujimori.

succession.value: Elections, interrupted by coups and by Congress impeaching or forcing out presidents.

institutions.value: Congress, which can impeach the president; the country is divided into 25 regions.

stability.value: Insurgent groups such as the Shining Path carried out attacks across the country in the 1980s and 1990s.

eliteConflict.value: Congress repeatedly clashed with presidents and removed them, leading to unrest from 2022.

armyAndTech.value: Armed forces with a history of political involvement.

majorWars.value: War of the Pacific with Chile (1879–84), the bloodiest in its history; wars with Ecuador (1941, 1995).

territoryChange.value: Lost the department of Tarapacá and the provinces of Tacna and Arica to Chile after the War of the Pacific.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of the Andean Community and the Pacific Alliance.

inventions.value: Few major inventions; strong archaeology and potato research (International Potato Center).

scienceEducation.value: San Marcos University (1551) is the oldest continuously functioning university in the Americas.

openness.value: Shifted to free-market policies in the 1990s; free trade agreements with China, the EU, Japan and others.

communicationTransport.value: A small rail network, about 2,000 km in 2025.

religion.value: Mostly Roman Catholic, mixed with Indigenous traditions.

languageWriting.value: Spanish is official, along with Quechua and other Indigenous languages where they predominate.

artsArchitecture.value: Writers such as Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa; famous cuisine and music.

socialStructure.value: About 60% mestizo, 22% Quechua, 6% white, 4% black and 2% Aymara (2017 census).

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in the Inca heritage and Peruvian cuisine.

dailyLife.value: Dishes such as ceviche, anticuchos and pachamanca.

neighbours.value: Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia and Chile.

ideasReligions.value: Liberation theology began with the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez.

colonisation.value: A former Spanish colony (Viceroyalty of Peru).

riseSignals.value: San Martín declared independence on 28 July 1821; it was completed after the Battle of Ayacucho (1824).

peakPeriod.value: An economic boom from the 2000s made Peru one of the world’s fastest-growing economies.

declineSignals.value: Economic crisis in the late 1980s and political unrest from 2022.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Peru; Wikipedia: History of Peru.
